Main.sentence: Denver ( /ˈdɛnvər/ ⓘ ___E:DEN-vər U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Pronunciation_respelling_key)___ ) is the ___E:capital U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_capitals_in_the_United_States)___ and ___E:most populous city U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_municipalities_in_Colorado)___ of the U.S. state of ___E:Colorado U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colorado)___ .

Officially a ___E:consolidated city and county U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_municipalities_in_Colorado#Consolidated_city_and_county)___ , it is located in the ___E:South Platte River U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Platte_River)___ valley on the western edge of the ___E:High Plains U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_Plains_(United_States))___ , and is just east of the ___E:Front Range U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Front_Range)___ of the ___E:Rocky Mountains U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rocky_Mountains)___ .

Denver is the ___E:19th-most populous city U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_United_States_cities_by_population)___ in the United States and the fifth-most populous state capital, with a population of 715,522 at the ___E:2020 census U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census)___ .

The ___E:Denver metropolitan area U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denver_metropolitan_area)___ , with over 3.05 million residents, is the ___E:19th-largest metropolitan area U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_statistical_area)___ in the country and functions as the economic and cultural center of the broader ___E:Front Range Urban Corridor U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Front_Range_Urban_Corridor)___ .
Denver's downtown district lies about 12 miles (19 kilometers) east of the ___E:foothills U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foothills)___ of the Rocky Mountains.

Named after ___E:James W. Denver U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_W._Denver)___ , the governor of the ___E:Kansas Territory U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_Territory)___ at the time, Denver was founded at the confluence of ___E:Cherry Creek U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cherry_Creek_(Colorado))___ and the ___E:South Platte River U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Platte_River)___ in 1858 during the Gold Rush era. ___E:Nicknamed U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_city_nicknames_in_the_United_States)___ the "Mile High City" because its official elevation is exactly one mile (5280 feet or 1609.344 meters) above sea level, Denver grew beyond its prospecting origins to become the principal commercial and transportation hub for a broad region spanning the Great Plains and Rocky Mountain West. [a]  The ___E:105th meridian west of Greenwich U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/105th_meridian_west)___ , the longitudinal reference for the ___E:Mountain Time Zone U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mountain_Time_Zone)___ , passes directly through ___E:Denver Union Station U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denver_Union_Station)___ .

As the most populous metropolitan area in a 560-mile (900 km) radius, Denver is a major cultural hub with a variety of museums and cultural institutions, including the ___E:Denver Performing Arts Complex U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denver_Performing_Arts_Complex)___ and ___E:Denver Art Museum U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denver_Art_Museum)___ .

Denver also has ___E:professional sports teams U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_in_Denver)___ in ___E:all five major leagues U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Major_professional_sports_leagues_in_the_United_States_and_Canada)___ .
Denver's economy is diverse, with eight ___E:Fortune 500 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fortune_500)___ firms headquartered in the city.

The greater Denver area was inhabited by several Indigenous peoples such as ___E:Apaches U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apache)___ , ___E:Utes U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ute_people)___ , ___E:Cheyennes U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cheyenne)___ , ___E:Comanches U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comanche)___ , and ___E:Arapahoes U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arapaho)___ .

By the terms of the 1851 ___E:Treaty of Fort Laramie U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Fort_Laramie_(1851))___ between the United States and various tribes including the Cheyenne and Arapaho,  the United States unilaterally defined and recognized Cheyenne and Arapaho territory as ranging from the ___E:North Platte River U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Platte_River)___ in present-day ___E:Wyoming U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wyoming)___ and ___E:Nebraska U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nebraska)___ southward to the ___E:Arkansas River U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arkansas_River)___ in present-day Colorado and ___E:Kansas U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas)___ .
This definition specifically encompasses the land of modern Metropolitan Denver.

But the discovery in November 1858 of ___E:gold U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gold)___ in the ___E:Rocky Mountains U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rocky_Mountains)___ in Colorado  (then part of the western ___E:Kansas Territory U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_Territory)___ )  brought on a ___E:gold rush U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pikes_Peak_Gold_Rush)___ and a consequent flood of white immigration across Cheyenne and Arapaho lands.
Colorado territorial officials pressured federal authorities to redefine and reduce the extent of ___E:Indian U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Native_Americans_in_the_United_States)___ treaty lands.

In the summer of 1858, during the ___E:Pike's Peak Gold Rush U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pike%27s_Peak_Gold_Rush)___ , a group of gold prospectors from ___E:Lawrence, Kansas U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lawrence,_Kansas)___ , established ___E:Montana City U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montana_City,_Colorado)___ as a ___E:mining town U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mining_town)___ on the banks of the ___E:South Platte River U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Platte_River)___ in what was then western ___E:Kansas Territory U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_Territory)___ , on traditional lands of ___E:Cheyenne U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cheyenne)___ and ___E:Arapaho U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arapaho)___ .
This was the first historical settlement in what later became the city of Denver.

But the site faded quickly, and by the summer of 1859 it was abandoned in favor of ___E:Auraria U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auraria,_Denver)___ (named after the gold-mining town of ___E:Auraria, Georgia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auraria,_Georgia)___ ) and St. Charles City.

On November 22, 1858, [contradictory] ___E:General William Larimer U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Larimer_Jr.)___ and Captain Jonathan Cox, both land speculators from eastern ___E:Kansas Territory U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_Territory)___ , placed ___E:cottonwood U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Populus_sect._Aigeiros)___ logs to stake a claim on the bluff overlooking the confluence of the South Platte River and ___E:Cherry Creek U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cherry_Creek_(Colorado))___ , across the creek from the existing mining settlement of Auraria, and on the site of the existing townsite of St. Charles.
Larimer named the townsite Denver City to curry favor with Kansas Territorial Governor ___E:James W. Denver U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_W._Denver)___ .

Larimer hoped the town's name would help it be selected as the ___E:county seat U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/County_seat)___ of ___E:Arapahoe County U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arapahoe_County,_Colorado)___ , but unbeknownst to him, Governor Denver had already resigned from office.

The location was accessible to existing trails and was across the South Platte River from the site of seasonal encampments of the ___E:Cheyenne U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cheyenne)___ and ___E:Arapaho U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arapaho)___ .

The site of these first towns is now occupied by ___E:Confluence Park U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Confluence_Park)___ near downtown Denver. ___E:Edward W. Wynkoop U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_W._Wynkoop)___ came to Colorado in 1859 and became one of the city's founders.
Wynkoop Street in Denver is named after him.
Larimer, along with associates in the St. Charles City Land Company, sold parcels in the town to merchants and miners, with the intention of creating a major city that would cater to new immigrants.
Denver City was a frontier town, with an economy based on servicing local miners with gambling, saloons, livestock, and goods trading.
In the early years, land parcels were often traded for grubstakes or gambled away by miners in Auraria.
In May 1859, Denver City residents donated 53 lots to the Leavenworth & Pike's Peak Express in order to secure the region's first overland wagon route.

Offering daily service for "passengers, mail, freight, and gold", the Express reached Denver on a trail that trimmed westward travel time from twelve days to six. The ___E:Denver City, Kansas Territory U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denver_City,_Kansas_Territory)___ , post office opened on February 11, 1860

On February 18, 1861, six chiefs of the Southern Cheyenne and four of the Arapaho signed the ___E:Treaty of Fort Wise U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Fort_Wise)___ with the United States  at ___E:Bent's New Fort U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bent%27s_New_Fort)___ at ___E:Big Timbers U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Timbers)___ near what is now ___E:Lamar, Colorado U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lamar,_Colorado)___ .
They ceded more than 90 percent of the lands designated for them by the Fort Laramie Treaty, including the area of modern Denver.

Some Cheyennes opposed to the treaty, saying that it had been signed by a small minority of the chiefs without the consent or approval of the rest of the tribe, that the signatories had not understood what they signed, and that they had been bribed to sign by a large distribution of gifts.
The territorial government of Colorado, however, claimed the treaty was a "solemn obligation" and considered that those Indians who refused to abide by it were hostile and planning a war.

On February 28, 1861, the ___E:Colorado Territory U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colorado_Territory)___ was created,  ___E:Arapahoe County U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arapahoe_County,_Colorado_Territory)___ was formed on November 1, 1861,  and Denver City was incorporated on November 7, 1861.  Denver City served as the Arapahoe County Seat from 1861 until ___E:consolidation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Consolidated_city-county)___ in 1902.  With its newfound importance, Denver City shortened its name to Denver in 1866.  On December 9, 1867, Denver became the ___E:territorial capital U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_city)___ .
On August 1, 1876, Colorado was ___E:admitted to the Union U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_U.S._states_by_date_of_statehood)___ .
Denver was made the permanent state capital in a ___E:1881 Colorado state capital referendum U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1881_Colorado_state_capital_referendum)___ .

This disagreement on the validity of ___E:Treaty of Fort Wise U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Fort_Wise)___ escalated to bring about the ___E:Colorado War U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colorado_War)___ of 1864 and 1865, during which the brutal ___E:Sand Creek massacre U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sand_Creek_massacre)___ against ___E:Cheyenne U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cheyenne)___ and ___E:Arapaho U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arapaho)___ peoples occurred.

The aftermath of the war was the dissolution of the reservation in Eastern Colorado, the signing of ___E:Medicine Lodge Treaty U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medicine_Lodge_Treaty)___ which stipulated that the ___E:Cheyenne U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cheyenne)___ and ___E:Arapaho U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arapaho)___ peoples would be relocated outside of their traditional territory.
This treaty term was achieved, even though the treaty was not legally ratified by the tribal members, as per the treaty's own terms.
Thus, by the end of 1860s, this effectively and completely cleared the Denver area of its indigenous inhabitants.

Although by the close of the 1860s Denver residents could look with pride at their success establishing a vibrant supply and service center, the decision to route the nation's first transcontinental railroad through ___E:Cheyenne City U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cheyenne,_Wyoming)___ , rather than Denver, threatened the prosperity of the young town. The transcontinental railroad passed a daunting 100 miles (160 kilometers) away, but citizens mobilized to build a railroad to connect Denver to it. Spearheaded by visionary leaders, including Territorial Governor ___E:John Evans U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Evans_(Colorado_governor))___ , ___E:David Moffat U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Moffat)___ , and ___E:Walter Cheesman U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Cheesman)___ , fundraising began.
Within three days, $300,000 had been raised, and citizens were optimistic.
Fundraising stalled before enough was raised, forcing these visionary leaders to take control of the debt-ridden railroad.

Despite challenges, on June 24, 1870, citizens cheered as the ___E:Denver Pacific U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denver_Pacific)___ completed the link to the transcontinental railroad, ushering in a new age of prosperity for Denver.
Finally linked to the rest of the nation by rail, Denver prospered as a service and supply center.

The young city grew during these years, attracting millionaires with their mansions, as well as a mixture of crime and poverty of a rapidly growing city. Denver citizens were proud when the rich chose Denver and were thrilled when ___E:Horace Tabor U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Tabor)___ , the Leadville mining millionaire, built a business block at 16th and Larimer, as well as the elegant Tabor Grand Opera House.

Luxurious hotels, including the much-loved ___E:Brown Palace Hotel U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brown_Palace_Hotel_(Denver,_Colorado))___ , soon followed, as well as splendid homes for millionaires, such as the Croke, Patterson, Campbell Mansion at 11th and Pennsylvania and the now-demolished Moffat Mansion at 8th and Grant.
Intent on transforming Denver into one of the world's great cities, leaders wooed industry and attracted laborers to work in these factories.

Soon, in addition to the elite and a large middle class, Denver had a growing population of immigrant German, Italian, and Chinese laborers, soon followed by African Americans from the Deep South and Hispanic workers.
The influx of the new residents strained available housing.
In addition, the Silver Crash of 1893 unsettled political, social, and economic balances.
Competition among the different ethnic groups was often expressed as bigotry, and social tensions gave rise to the ___E:Red Scare U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Scare)___ .
Americans were suspicious of immigrants, who were sometimes allied with socialist and labor union causes.
After World War I, a revival of the ___E:Ku Klux Klan U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ku_Klux_Klan)___ attracted white, native-born Americans who were anxious about the many changes in society.
Unlike the earlier organization that was active in the rural South, KKK chapters developed in urban areas of the Midwest and West, including Denver, and into Idaho and Oregon.
Corruption and crime also developed in Denver.

Between 1880 and 1895, the city underwent a huge rise in corruption, as crime bosses, such as ___E:Soapy Smith U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soapy_Smith)___ , worked side by side with elected officials and the police to control elections, gambling, and ___E:bunco gangs U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lou_Blonger)___ .
The city also suffered a ___E:depression in 1893 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denver_Depression_of_1893)___ after the crash of silver prices.

In 1887, the precursor to the international charity ___E:United Way U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Way_of_America)___ was formed in Denver by local religious leaders, who raised funds and coordinated various charities to help Denver's poor.  By 1890, Denver had grown to be the second-largest city west of ___E:Omaha, Nebraska U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Omaha,_Nebraska)___ .
In 1900, whites represented 96.8% of Denver's population.
The African American and Hispanic populations increased with migrations of the 20th century.
Many African Americans first came as workers on the railroad, which had a terminus in Denver, and began to settle there.
Between the 1880s and 1930s, Denver's floriculture industry developed and thrived.
This period became known locally as the ___E:Carnation Gold Rush U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carnation_Gold_Rush)___ .

A bill proposing a state constitutional amendment to allow ___E:home rule U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Home_rule)___ for Denver and other municipalities was introduced in the legislature in 1901 and passed.

The measure called for a statewide referendum, which voters approved in 1902. On December 1 that year, Governor ___E:James Orman U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Orman)___ proclaimed the amendment part of the state's fundamental law. The City and County of Denver came into being on that date and was separated from Arapahoe and Adams counties.

From 1953 to 1989, the ___E:Rocky Flats Plant U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rocky_Flats_Plant)___ , a ___E:DOE U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Energy)___ nuclear weapon facility that was about 15 miles from Denver, produced ___E:fissile U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fissile)___ ___E:plutonium U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plutonium)___ " ___E:pits U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pit_(nuclear_weapon))___ " for ___E:nuclear warheads U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_warhead)___ .

A major fire at the facility in 1957, as well as leakage from ___E:nuclear waste U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_waste)___ stored at the site between 1958 and 1968, resulted in the ___E:contamination of some parts of Denver U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radioactive_contamination_from_the_Rocky_Flats_Plant)___ , to varying degrees, with ___E:plutonium-239 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plutonium-239)___ , a harmful radioactive substance with a half-life of 24,200 years.

A 1981 study by the Jefferson County health director, Carl Johnson, linked the contamination to an increase in birth defects and ___E:cancer U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cancer)___ incidence in central Denver and nearer Rocky Flats.
Later studies confirmed many of his findings.
Plutonium contamination was still present outside the former plant site as of August 2010 [update] .
It presents risks to building the envisioned Jefferson Parkway,  which would complete Denver's automotive ___E:beltway U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_road)___ .

In 1970, Denver was selected to host the ___E:1976 Winter Olympics U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1976_Winter_Olympics)___ to coincide with Colorado's centennial celebration, but in November 1972, Colorado voters struck down ballot initiatives allocating public funds to pay for the high costs of the games.
They were moved to ___E:Innsbruck U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Innsbruck)___ , Austria.
The notoriety of being the only city ever to decline to host an Olympiad after being selected has made subsequent bids difficult.
The movement against hosting the games was based largely on environmental issues and was led by State Representative ___E:Richard Lamm U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Lamm)___ .
He was subsequently elected to three terms (1975–87) as ___E:Colorado governor U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Colorado_Governors)___ .
Denver explored a potential bid for the ___E:2022 Winter Olympics U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Winter_Olympics)___ ,  but no bid was submitted.

In 2010, Denver adopted a comprehensive update of its zoning code,  which was developed to guide development as envisioned in adopted plans such as Blueprint Denver,  Transit Oriented Development Strategic Plan, Greenprint Denver, and the Strategic Transportation Plan.

Denver has hosted the ___E:Democratic National Convention U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_National_Convention)___ twice, in ___E:1908 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1908_Democratic_National_Convention)___ and ___E:2008 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_Democratic_National_Convention)___ .
It promoted the city on the national, political, and socioeconomic stage.

On August 10–15, 1993, Denver hosted the Catholic Church's ___E:6th World Youth Day U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Youth_Day_1993)___ , which was attended by an estimated 500,000, making it the largest gathering in Colorado history.
In 2015, a new commuter railway system commenced operations in the Denver metropolitan area with a network operation of 25 kV 60 Hz.

Denver has been known historically as the Queen City of the Plains and the Queen City of the West , because of its important role in the ___E:agricultural U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agriculture_in_the_United_States)___ industry of the ___E:High Plains U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_Plains_(United_States))___ region in eastern Colorado and along the foothills of the ___E:Colorado Front Range U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colorado_Front_Range)___ .

Denver is in the center of the ___E:Front Range Urban Corridor U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Front_Range_Urban_Corridor)___ , between the ___E:Rocky Mountains U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rocky_Mountains)___ to the west and the ___E:High Plains U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_Plains_(United_States))___ to the east. Its topography consists of plains in the city center with hilly areas to the north, west, and south.
It is the only state capital in the United States that is a consolidated city-county.

At the ___E:2020 United States census U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census)___ , the City and County of Denver had an area of 99,025 acres (400.739 km 2 ), including 1,057 acres (4.276 km 2 ) of water.

The City and County of Denver is surrounded by three other counties: ___E:Adams County U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adams_County,_Colorado)___ to the north and east, ___E:Arapahoe County U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arapahoe_County,_Colorado)___ to the south and east, and ___E:Jefferson County U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jefferson_County,_Colorado)___ to the west.

Denver's nickname is the "Mile-High City", as its official elevation is one mile (5,280 ft; 1,609 m) above sea level, defined by the elevation of the spot of a benchmark on the steps of the State Capitol building.
The elevation of the entire city ranges from 5,130 to 5,690 feet (1,560 to 1,730 m).
The City and County of Denver has 78 official ___E:neighborhoods U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neighborhood)___ used for planning and administration.

The system of neighborhood boundaries and names dates to 1970 when city planners divided the city into 73 groups of one to four census tracts, called "statistical neighborhoods," most of which are unchanged since then.
Unlike some other cities, such as ___E:Chicago U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Community_areas_in_Chicago)___ , Denver does not have official larger area designations.
Colloquially, names such as Northside and Westside are still in use, but not well-known.
Community planners have recently been using a set of 19 larger areas, all of which are groups of statistical neighborhoods, as part of the Area Planning process.
Denver also has a number of colloquial neighborhood names and boundaries reflecting how people in an area, or others such as community groups and real estate developers, have defined areas.

Well-known non-administrative neighborhoods include the historic and trendy ___E:LoDo U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LoDo)___ (short for "Lower Downtown"), part of the city's ___E:Union Station neighborhood U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_Station,_Denver)___ ; Uptown, straddling ___E:North Capitol Hill U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Capitol_Hill,_Denver,_Colorado)___ and ___E:City Park West U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_Park_West,_Denver)___ ; Curtis Park and RiNo ("River North"), both part of the ___E:Five Points U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Five_Points_(Denver))___ neighborhood; ___E:Alamo Placita U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alamo_Placita,_Denver)___ , the northern part of the ___E:Speer neighborhood U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speer,_Denver)___ ; ___E:Park Hill U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Park_Hill,_Denver)___ , a successful example of intentional racial integration;  and ___E:Golden Triangle U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Triangle,_Denver)___ , in the Civic Center.

One of Denver's newer neighborhoods was built on the site of ___E:Stapleton International Airport U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stapleton_International_Airport)___ , named after former Denver mayor ___E:Benjamin F. Stapleton U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benjamin_F._Stapleton)___ , a member of the Ku Klux Klan.  In 2020, the neighborhood's community association voted to change the name from Stapleton to Central Park  (see more in Politics section below).
The Central Park neighborhood itself has 12 "neighborhoods" within its boundaries.

Denver features a ___E:cool semi-arid climate U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continental_semi-arid_climate)___ ( ___E:Köppen climate classification U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K%C3%B6ppen_climate_classification)___ : BSk , ___E:Trewartha U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trewartha_climate_classification)___ : BSao ) with generally low humidity and around 3,100 hours of sunshine per year, although humid ___E:microclimates U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microclimate)___ can be found nearby depending on exact location.
These humid microclimates have the temperature of a hot-summer humid continental climate (Koppen: Dfa ) or a humid subtropical climate (Koppen: Cfa ) when using the −3 °C (27 °F) isotherm.
It has four distinct seasons and receives most of its precipitation from April through August.

Due to its inland location on the ___E:High Plains U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_Plains_(United_States))___ , at the foot of the ___E:Rocky Mountains U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rocky_Mountains)___ , the region can be subject to sudden changes in weather.
July is the warmest month, with an average high temperature of 89.9 °F (32.2 °C).
Summers range from warm to hot with occasional, sometimes severe, afternoon thunderstorms and high temperatures reaching 90 °F (32 °C) on 38 days annually, and occasionally 100 °F (38 °C).
December, the coldest month of the year, has an average daily high temperature of 44 °F (6.7 °C).

Winters consist of periods of snow and very low temperatures alternating with periods of milder weather due to the warming effect of ___E:Chinook winds U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinook_wind)___ .
In winter, daytime highs occasionally exceed 60 °F (16 °C), but they also often fail to reach 32 °F (0 °C) during periods of cold weather.
Occasionally, daytime highs can even fail to rise above 0 °F (−18 °C) due to arctic air masses.
On the coldest nights of the year, lows can fall to −10 °F (−23 °C) or below, with the city experiencing a low of −24 °F (−31 °C) on December 22, 2022, with a wind chill of −40 °F (−40 °C).

Snowfall is common throughout the late fall, winter and early spring, averaging 53.5 inches (136 cm) for 1981–2010;  but in the 2021 winter season, Denver began the month of December without any snowfall for the first time in history.

The average window for measurable (≥0.1 in or 0.25 cm) snow is October 17 through April 27; however, measurable snowfall has occurred as early as September 4 and as late as June 3.  Extremes in temperature range from −29 °F (−34 °C) on January 9, 1875, up to 105 °F (41 °C) as recently as June 28, 2018.  Due to the city's high elevation and aridity, ___E:diurnal temperature variation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diurnal_temperature_variation)___ is large throughout the year.

___E:Tornadoes U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado)___ are rare west of the I-25 corridor; one notable exception was an ___E:F3 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fujita_scale)___ tornado that struck 4.4 miles (7.1 km) south of downtown on June 15, 1988. Avenues north of Ellsworth are numbered (with the exception of Colfax Avenue and several others, such as Martin Luther King, Jr. Blvd and Montview Blvd.), while avenues south of Ellsworth are named.

There is also an older downtown grid system that was designed to be parallel to the confluence of the ___E:South Platte River U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Platte_River)___ and ___E:Cherry Creek U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cherry_Creek_(Colorado))___ .
Most of the streets downtown and in ___E:LoDo U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LoDo)___ run northeast–southwest and northwest–southeast.
This system has an unplanned benefit for snow removal; if the streets were in a normal N–S/E–W grid, only the N–S streets would receive sunlight.
With the grid oriented to the diagonal directions, the NW–SE streets receive sunlight to melt snow in the morning and the NE–SW streets receive it in the afternoon.
This idea was from Henry Brown the founder of the ___E:Brown Palace Hotel U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brown_Palace_Hotel_(Denver,_Colorado))___ .

There is now a plaque across the street from the ___E:Brown Palace Hotel U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brown_Palace_Hotel_(Denver,_Colorado))___ that honors this idea. The NW–SE streets are numbered, while the NE–SW streets are named.
The named streets start at the intersection of Colfax Avenue and Broadway with the block-long Cheyenne Place.
The numbered streets start underneath the Colfax and I-25 viaducts.
There are 27 named and 44 numbered streets on this grid. There are also a few vestiges of the old grid system in the normal grid, such as Park Avenue, Morrison Road, and Speer Boulevard.

Larimer Street, named after ___E:William Larimer Jr. U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Larimer_Jr.)___ , the founder of Denver, which is in the heart of ___E:LoDo U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LoDo)___ , is the oldest street in Denver.

All roads in the downtown grid system are streets (e.g., ___E:16th Street U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/16th_Street_Mall)___ , Stout Street), except for the five NE–SW roads nearest the intersection of Colfax Avenue and Broadway: Cheyenne Place, Cleveland Place, Court Place, Tremont Place and Glenarm Place.
Roads outside that system that travel east–west are designated "avenues" and those that travel north–south are designated "streets" (e.g., Colfax Avenue, Lincoln Street).
Boulevards are higher capacity streets and travel any direction (more commonly north and south).
Smaller roads are sometimes referred to as places, drives (though not all drives are smaller capacity roads; some are major thoroughfares), or courts.
Most streets outside the area between Broadway and Colorado Boulevard are organized alphabetically from the city's center.
East of Colorado Boulevard, the naming convention of streets takes on a predictable pattern of going through the alphabet by using each letter twice (i.e.
AA, BB, CC, DD, through YY – there is no Z).
The first street is almost always named after a plant or fruit, the second street is almost always named after a foreign place or location.
For example, Jersey Street / Jasmine Street, Quebec Street / Quince Street, and Syracuse Street / Spruce Street.
Inexplicably, the letter Y only has one street (Yosemite), and there is no Z. This double-alphabet naming convention continues in some form into Aurora, Colorado.

Some Denver streets have ___E:bicycle lanes U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bicycle_lanes)___ , leaving a patchwork of disjointed routes throughout the city. There are over 850 miles (1,370 km)  of paved, off-road, bike paths in Denver parks and along bodies of water, like Cherry Creek and the South Platte.

This allows for a significant portion of Denver's population to be bicycle commuters and has led to Denver being known as a bicycle-friendly city.  Some residents strongly oppose bike lanes, which has caused some plans to be watered down or nixed.
The review process for one bike line on Broadway will last over a year before city council members will make a decision.

In addition to the many bike paths, Denver launched B-Cycle – a citywide bicycle sharing program – in late April 2010. The B-Cycle network was the largest in the United States at the time of its launch, boasting 400 bicycles.
The ___E:Denver Boot U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wheel_clamp)___ , a car-disabling device, was first used in Denver.

The ___E:League of American Bicyclists U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/League_of_American_Bicyclists)___ rated Colorado as the sixth most bicycle-friendly state in the nation for 2024. This is due in large part to Front Range cities like Boulder, Fort Collins and Denver placing an emphasis on legislation, programs and infrastructure developments that promote cycling as a mode of transportation.  ___E:Walk Score U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walk_Score)___ has rated Denver as the fourth most bicycle-friendly large city in the United States.

According to data from the 2011 American Community Survey, Denver ranks 6th among US cities with populations over 400,000 in terms of the percentage of ___E:workers who commute by bicycle U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_U.S._cities_with_most_bicycle_commuters)___ at 2.2% of commuters.
B-Cycle – Denver's citywide bicycle sharing program – was the largest in the United States at the time of its launch in 2010, boasting 400 bicycles.
B-Cycle ridership peaked in 2014, then steadily declined.
The program announced it would cease operations at the end of January 2020.    The city announced plans to seek one or more new contractors to run a bike-share program starting mid-2020.
In 2018, ___E:electric scooter U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motorized_scooter)___ services began to place scooters in Denver.
Hundreds of unsanctioned LimeBike and Bird electric scooters appeared on Denver streets in May, causing an uproar.

In June, the city ordered the companies to remove them  and acted quickly to create an official program, including a requirement that scooters be left at RTD stops and out of the public right-of-way. Lime and Bird scooters then reappeared in late July, with limited compliance. ___E:Uber U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uber)___ 's Jump e-bikes arrived in late August, followed by ___E:Lyft U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lyft)___ 's nationwide electric scooter launch in early September.
Lyft says that it will, each night, take the scooters to the warehouse for safety checks, maintenance and charging.
Additionally, Spin and Razor each were permitted to add 350 scooters.
2017 rankings by ___E:Walk Score U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walk_Score)___ placed Denver twenty-sixth among 108 U.S. cities with a population of 200,000 or greater.
City leaders have acknowledged the concerns of walkability advocates that Denver has serious gaps in its sidewalk network.
The 2019 "Denver Moves: Pedestrians" plan outlines a need for approximate $1.3 billion in sidewalk funding, plus $400 million for trails.

In 2022, Denver voters passed Initiative 307, dubbed "Denver Deserves Sidewalks", to complete sidewalk construction and repair by shifting responsibility for sidewalk maintenance from property owners to the city and imposing a new fee on property owners based on the length of a property's sidewalk frontage,  although the measure may be revised in the course of implementation.
In 2015, 9.6 percent of Denver households lacked a car, and in 2016, this was virtually unchanged (9.4 percent).
The national average was 8.7 percent in 2016. Denver averaged 1.62 cars per household in 2016, compared to a national average of 1.8.

Denver is primarily served by the interstate freeways ___E:I-25 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interstate_25_(Colorado))___ and ___E:I-70 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interstate_70_(Colorado))___ .

The problematic intersection of the two interstates is referred to locally as " ___E:the mousetrap U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mousetrap_(Denver))___ " because, when viewed from the air, the junction (and subsequent vehicles) resemble mice in a large trap.
Denver also has a nearly complete beltway known as "the 470's".

These are ___E:SH 470 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SH_470_(CO))___ (also known as C-470), a freeway in the southwest Metro area, and two toll highways, ___E:E-470 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/E-470)___ (from southeast to northeast) and ___E:Northwest Parkway U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northwest_Parkway)___ (from terminus of E-470 to ___E:US 36 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Highway_36_(Colorado))___ ).

SH 470 was intended to be I-470 and built with federal highway funds, but the funding was redirected to complete conversion of downtown Denver's ___E:16th Street U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/16th_Street_Mall)___ to a pedestrian mall. As a result, construction was delayed until 1980 after state and local legislation was passed.
I-470 was also once called "The Silver Stake Highway", from Gov. Lamm's declared intention to drive a silver stake through it and kill it.

The project also includes a light rail line that traverses from downtown to the south end of the metro area at Lincoln Avenue.

The project spanned almost 19 miles (31 km) along the highway with an additional line traveling parallel to part of ___E:I-225 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interstate_225_(Colorado))___ , stopping just short of Parker Road.

Denver's early years as a major train hub of the west are still very visible today.

Trains stop in Denver at historic ___E:Union Station U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_Station_(Denver))___ , where travelers can access RTD's 16th Street Free MallRide or use light rail to tour the city. ___E:Union Station U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_Station_(Denver))___ will also serve as the main juncture for rail travel in the metro area, at the completion of ___E:FasTracks U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FasTracks)___ .
The city also plans to invest billions to bringing frequent public transit within one-fourth of a mile of most of its residents.

The average amount of time people spend commuting on public transit in Denver and Boulder, Colorado—for example, to and from work, on a weekday—is 77 minutes; 31% of public transit riders ride for more than two hours every day. The average amount of time people wait at a stop or station for public transit is 14 minutes, while 25% of riders wait for over 20 minutes, on average, every day. The average distance people usually ride in a single trip with public transit is 6.96 miles (11.20 km), while 31% travel over 7.46 miles (12.01 km) in a single direction.

Denver's relationship with ___E:Brest, France U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brest,_France)___ , began in 1948, making it the second-oldest ___E:sister city U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sister_city)___ in the United States.
In 1947, Amanda Knecht, a teacher at East High School, visited World War II–ravaged Brest.
When she returned, she shared her experiences in the city with her students, and her class raised $32,000 to help rebuild the children's wing of Brest's hospital.
The gift led to the development of the sister city program with Brest.
